entries.title: Pumpkin Patches and Rom-Coms: How the Commanders Moved Past Sunday’s Tie
entries.summary: After their frustrating tie with the Giants, Washington’s players did their best to put it out of their minds and focus on Monday’s matchup with the 49ers.
entries.content:
Amik Robertson was not in a good mood after the Commanders’ 27-27 tie with the Giants on Sunday.

The cornerback was penalized three times, including a ticky-tacky defensive pass interference call that wiped out an interception he got late in the third quarter. “Bullshit,” was how he described the call.

But days later, Robertson felt much better and had since moved on from the Meltdown in Maryland. And what helped the 28-year-old Lousisana native get past that game?

Rom-coms, of course.

“I didn't want to watch ‘The Notebook,’” Robertson said. “I watched ‘Anyone But You.’”

The Giants game was a major letdown for Washington. They led by 14 points with just over 11 minutes left in the fourth quarter, and after getting in field goal range late in overtime, the Commanders let time run out in the game before they could even attempt the game-winning kick.

Head coach Dan Quinn called the tie “gutting.” Pro Bowl receiver Terry McLaurin said it stung. And star quarterback Jayden Daniels, who laid on the ground for crucial seconds on the final play, said the result sucked.

The team gave themselves a day to sit with the result, and after two days off ahead of a Monday Night Football matchup with the undefeated 49ers, they were eager to put Sunday’s tie behind them and move on to Week 6.

Each player had his own unique way of using the time off to help move on from one of the most disastrous endings in franchise history.

For some, their reprieve was television.

Robertson normally plays the Madden video game series in his free time, but it's hard to not think about football when you’re playing a football game. So he opted for the Glen Powell- and Sydney Sweeney-led “Anyone But You” to relax his mind.

Defensive lineman Deatrich Wise also uses television to relax. But when you have a 3-year-old son, you tend to have little control over the remote.

“Paw Patrol, Sesame Street, stuff like that,” Wise said of his off-day viewing habits. “Monster Jams. It’s usually what it is.”

Linebacker Kain Medrano visited a pumpkin patch in Frederick County, Maryland, with his girlfriend, who he said “gets very festive” during this time of year. It was an opportunity to give attention to something other than his job for the first time in weeks.

“You give football a break for a quick second, just focus on family, on stuff that you don't really get to focus on day in, day out,” said Medrano. “Just because you're here in the facility all the time.”

Spending time with loved ones was a common thread for other players.

Linebacker K’Lavon Chaisson said his 3-year-old daughter provides both an escape from football and the perspective that you don’t have to linger on the negative results.

“Being with my daughter, she don't really give me time to sit and sulk about the football games,” Chaisson said. “I'm coming home and trying to just break everything down and cleanse my mind of it, and she jumps right on my lap. She don't care about the outcome of the game. She wants to go outside, draw chalk on the ground and play hopscotch, whatever it may be.”

Receiver Treylon Burks shares two daughters with his wife, Shelby. He used his time away from the facility to be with them. That said, the Arkansas native has other hobbies he would’ve liked to partake in, but the topography of the D.C. area makes it a bit difficult.

“It ain't much hunting and fishing out here for me, so I'll just wait till I can get back home to do that,” he said.

As reassuring and supportive as family can be, the pain of defeat (or a tie) can be an itch they can never scratch. Left tackle Brandon Coleman spent time with his girlfriend, family and friends, but he couldn’t stop replaying Sunday’s game in his head.

“They try to distract, but at the end of the day we're all competitors,” Coleman said. “It's tough — especially from something like that — to not think about it and have those thoughts after a game.”

Quinn implored the team to take those feelings and apply them to the final 12 games of the season. While a letdown like Sunday could tear a team apart, Quinn believes the adversity they’ve faced this season can help.

“We identified we only played 30% of the season,” Quinn said. “There's so much that's in front of us, and it's going to be an absolute battle.”

For what felt like the first time in his three-year career, Daniels faced heavy criticism for his decision-making in the Giants game. No matter what happened leading up to the final play, it was Daniels who took the sack and laid on the ground with no urgency.

"Jayden Daniels probably cost my man Dan Quinn his job, to be honest with you," Packers linebacker Micah Parsons said on his podcast this week.

Daniels said he leaned on his circle, including his parents, to move past the result. But more importantly, the 2024 Rookie of the Year award winner got back to work. He lifted weights, watched the Giants film and then got a jump start on studying the 49ers defense.

This may have been the lowest moment of his young career, but Daniels understands that dwelling on the tie or what he could have done differently won’t magically change the team’s 1-3-1 record.

“You still think about stuff like that, right?” he said. “But it can't help me. It can help me moving forward … I can't dwell on the past too much, because I got a game on Monday night to worry about.”
entries.author: Martenzie Johnson

entries.title: Trump Waives New Russia Sanctions, Citing National Interest
entries.summary: Named after late Sen. Lindsey Graham, the bill had sought to clamp down on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.
entries.content:
By Will Weissert and Meg Kinnard

President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest.

Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. It drew shift condemnation from congressional Democrats.

Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.

Trump's unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.

An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president's handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump's approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress after midterm elections on Nov. 3.

Sanctions were seen as part of Graham's legacy

Graham, a close ally and friend of the president, had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July. He had advocated for stricter U.S. sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine.

His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation — then changed his mind Friday.

The package had been meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbor more than four years ago. The bill, also drafted by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.

It also directed Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

Blumenthal said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on "the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies.”

“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said.

Democratic Virginia Rep. Don Beyer noted on social media shortly after the announcement of the sanctions being suspended that he and others had “warned" Trump might make such a move. The veteran congressman, who spoke out against the bill as it was debated, called on Congress to “fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine.”

The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest. The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress.

Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting.

The Trump administration, meanwhile, had remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large majorities in the House and Senate following Graham’s sudden death — with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy.

Trump's action follows announced diesel deal with Putin

Under last week's agreement, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”

Trump’s striking a diesel deal with Putin has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine -- without making a different to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war on Iran.

The sanctions that Trump has now suspended, meanwhile, also had become a campaign centerpiece for Sen. Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who was appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term. She is now running to replace him in the Senate more permanently.

Darline Graham said in a statement after Trump signed the bill, “I wish Lindsey were here to celebrate this historic day." In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham — who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week — said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed.

She acknowledged, however, that it was the president’s purview as to how he implemented it.

“It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia. “So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.”
entries.author: The Associated Press
